chapter_name: The World is too Much With Us
learning_objective: 🎯 Critique the modern obsession with money! Understand Wordsworth's passionate plea to stop destroying nature in the name of industrial progress and materialism.

key_vocabulary.hindi_meaning: प्रकृति-पूजक (जो पुराने देवी-देवताओं को मानता हो)

main_concepts.simple_explanation: Wordsworth complains that humanity is completely consumed by 'getting' (making money) and 'spending' (buying things). We are wasting our lives and our inner powers on materialism, losing touch with what truly matters.

We no longer see the beauty of the sea shining in the moonlight or hear the howling winds. The poet says we have 'given our hearts away' in a 'sordid boon' (a dirty blessing)—trading our souls for industrial progress.
The poet claims we are 'out of tune' with nature. Things that should move us emotionally—like a beautiful landscape—no longer have any effect on us because we only care about money and factories.

In a moment of frustration, the poet cries out that he would rather be a 'Pagan'—an ancient person who worshipped nature gods—than a modern, soulless Christian. At least a Pagan standing in a meadow would feel magic, seeing sea gods like Proteus and Triton!

fun_activity.title: 📱 The Screen-Time Audit
fun_activity.instructions: Wordsworth complained about people ignoring nature for money in the 1800s. Today, it's screens! Check your phone's 'Screen Time' app. How many hours did you spend 'getting and spending' digital attention today? Could you have spent one of those hours looking at the sky?

exam_tips: 📌 Structure: It is a Petrarchan Sonnet. The first 8 lines (Octave) present the problem (our materialism), and the last 6 lines (Sestet) present the poet's emotional reaction (wishing to be a Pagan).
📌 'Sordid boon' is a vital oxymoron. It means a 'dirty gift'—industrialization gave us wealth (a boon), but it dirtied our souls and the environment (sordid).
📌 The mythological allusions to Proteus and Triton emphasize a time when humans saw divinity and magic in nature, contrasting with modern scientific/industrial coldness.
quick_recap: ⭐ The poem is a strong critique of the First Industrial Revolution.
⭐ Wordsworth believes that without a connection to nature, humanity becomes spiritually dead.
⭐ Nature is personified beautifully (the Sea baring her bosom to the moon).
